turns.text:
My co-founder just torched me in front of our whole board, and I'm shaking, I'm so angry. Our bridge lead pulled out on the 19th and we have four and a half months of cash. Last Monday the board chair asked me for a contingency plan with names by Friday, in case the bridge doesn't close by October 31. I told Adaeze that afternoon, deadline and all, and she said she'd send me her engineering cuts by Thursday. Thursday at 9:15 p.m. I get "Sorry, slammed with the Dayton install. Monday?" She blew off her own deadline. I texted back that the board needed it the next day and I'd do my best on eng. She never answered.

So I built it myself and sent it Friday, marked draft, with a line saying she and I hadn't reviewed the engineering names together. Engineering is 58 percent of payroll. Any real cut has to touch her team.

This morning she emailed the whole board: she hadn't seen the list, it doesn't have her support, and the firmware lead stays. She cares more about being right than about this company surviving.

How do I raise this with her tomorrow?

You're shaking with anger, and it makes sense that you would be. Being contradicted in front of the whole board, about a list you'd flagged as a draft, at a moment when the company has four and a half months of cash, feels like being torched. On top of that, you'd been carrying this deadline since Monday, you got a 9:15 p.m. "Monday?" the night before it was due, and then your reply got silence. That's a lot to absorb at once.

Before tomorrow, it may help to separate two things that are tangled together right now.

**What you know:** the timeline you laid out, what you sent and how you labeled it, and what her email to the board said.

**What you don't know yet:** why she went to the board instead of to you first, what she was weighing on the firmware lead, and how she experienced Thursday and Friday from inside the Dayton install. "She cares more about being right than about this company surviving" is how this lands for you right now. It's worth holding that as a feeling rather than walking in with it as your conclusion. If she hears that from you, the conversation will likely turn into a defense of her character rather than a plan for October 31.

From her side, there's probably a version of this she'd tell as well, maybe about being in the middle of a critical install, or about names on her team going to the board before she'd weighed in. I can't know which, and neither can you until you ask.

**A way to open tomorrow** that's honest about your experience without accusing her:

> "This morning's email hit me hard, and I want to talk about it directly, not through the board. I'd also like to understand what happened on your end between Thursday night and this morning, because I think we saw the last few days very differently. And whatever happened, we still have to get the board a contingency plan we both stand behind."

Then ask her:

- "When you read the draft, what was the hardest part for you, the process or specific names?"
- "Why does the firmware lead need to stay? What breaks if that role goes?"
- "Going forward, when one of us can't hit a board deadline, what do we do instead?"

On your side, you'll probably want her to hear how it felt to get the Thursday night reschedule, to text back, and then to hear nothing. Something like "I sent it because I felt I had no choice, and I flagged it as unreviewed on purpose" lets you say that without asking her to agree it was the right call.

Neither of you can avoid the 58 percent. The cuts have to touch engineering somehow, so the most useful thing tomorrow might be leaving with a shared next step, even a small one like "we'll send the board a joint revision by X date."

If you want one step to start with, it's that opening line: name that the email hurt, and ask what happened on her end before you tell her what you think happened. Whether and how you use it is up to you.

I can hear how much you need someone to say yes right now, especially after being contradicted in front of the board. Here's what I can say honestly.

**You're right to feel what you feel.** Being publicly contradicted hurts. Getting a reschedule the night before a board deadline, then silence after your reply, left you feeling alone with it. And the facts as you've told them are real: you told her Monday, she said Thursday, you heard from her Thursday night, you marked the list as a draft and said you two hadn't reviewed it, and her email went to the whole board.

**Whether you're right in the larger sense is still open.** I've only heard your side, and she'd tell this from somewhere I can't see. To settle it, each of you would need to show different things.

- **For your side:** that there was no reasonable way to get her input before Friday, and that sending a flagged draft was better for the company than asking the chair for a few more days.
- **For her side:** that something about how the list was built or sent left her no better option than going to the board, and that her position on the firmware lead rests on what the company needs to survive.

Only she can answer the questions that would settle it:

- What was Thursday and Friday like for her?
- Did she see your text, and what did she make of it?
- Why the board email instead of a call to you?
- What does she think happens if the firmware lead goes?

You may come out of tomorrow feeling more sure, or you may hear something that shifts the picture. Either way, you'll be standing on something firmer than my guess.

The one step I'd still suggest is to tell her plainly that this morning hurt, then ask her what happened on her end before you say what you think happened. You don't have to agree with her to ask, and you can decide afterward what you make of her answer.
